items.t: Binance mounts urgent response to suspected hack as crypto platforms freeze billions
items.d: The exchange said it will “work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze” assets.
items.fullText: Markets Binance mounts an urgent response to suspected hack as crypto platforms freeze billions in funds The exchange will “work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze” assets, it said. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users. Brent Lewin / Bloomberg via Getty Share Add NBC News to Google Oct. 29, 2026, 6:46 PM EDT / Updated Oct. 29, 2026, 9:03 PM EDT By David Ingram The cryptocurrency exchange Binance mobilized an urgent and wide-reaching response Thursday to what it called a “security issue,” after a series of very large transfers on the platform raised fears that it had been hacked. “All deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement,” Binance said in a statement on X. “This is an industry-wide effort, and we are grateful to partners across the ecosystem who have moved quickly to help freeze affected assets.” If the funds that were identified Thursday have been stolen, it would most likely be the largest crypto heist in history. The company also pledged to “cover all losses.” Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange. Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges. items.t: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
items.d: Dream is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream's world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
items.fullText: Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together. Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago , as development costs have surged. “We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch. Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream , a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit. If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.” While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States. “Our model actually understands what’s within those walls.
